query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-throughput computational screening combined with a controlled annealing treatment can be used to stabilize desired phases, refine microstructure, and optimize the high‐temperature mechanical properties of high‐entropy alloys by tailoring the formation of load-bearing nanoscale precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase high-entropy alloy system (e.g., an Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary alloy) with regions prone to forming either nanoscale ordered precipitates or antiphase domains depending on slight compositional deviations.
generation.intervention: Apply high-throughput computational screening to predict the composition and heat-treatment (annealing) parameters that favor the formation of finely dispersed, ordered L21 precipitates, followed by experimental processing (arc melting, homogenization, and annealing) to validate the predictions.
generation.conditions: Use processing steps such as repeated arc melting for homogeneity, high-temperature homogenization (e.g., ~1200 °C), and controlled annealing at a lower temperature (e.g., ~700 °C for 2 hours) within the compositional range where Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%.
generation.structural_mediator: The morphology (nanoscale precipitates versus antiphase domains) and distribution of the L21-ordered phase in the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Tailoring processing parameters based on computational predictions alters the thermodynamic driving force for ordering, thereby controlling precipitate size, coherency, and volume fraction. Finer, load-bearing precipitates enable better load transfer and enhanced precipitation strengthening compared to coarser or less coherent phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized alloy will exhibit a well-defined, nanoscale L21 precipitate distribution in the matrix and demonstrate improved high-temperature yield strength compared to alloys processed without such targeted intervention.
generation.baseline: Alloys produced without computationally guided processing tend to form less controlled microstructures (e.g., dominant antiphase domains or coarser precipitates), resulting in lower high-temperature yield strength.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be most effective in alloy systems within a limited compositional window and where current thermodynamic databases offer reliable predictions; outside this window or with significant database inaccuracies, the improvements may not materialize.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements depend on the accuracy of the high-throughput screening predictions and the fidelity of the thermodynamic database; discrepancies may arise if the models do not capture all kinetic or compositional complexities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples near the predicted optimal composition via arc melting. Process one set using the computationally guided annealing schedule (homogenization followed by a controlled annealing step at ~700 °C for 2 hours) and the other using a conventional, non-optimized heat treatment. Characterize both sets for phase composition (using XRD), precipitate morphology and size (using TEM), and measure high-temperature yield strength (via compression testing at temperatures around 600–700 °C).
measurements: TEM for precipitate size distribution and morphology
Volume fraction analysis of L21 precipitates vs. antiphase domains
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the computationally guided process does not result in a statistically significant refinement in precipitate morphology (i.e., a higher volume fraction of nanoscale L21 precipitates) and does not enhance yield strength compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the proposed hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
